summary: The way an LDP speaker advertises labels for a Forwarding Equivalence Class depends on the FEC type, not necessarily on the session's negotiated mode. This document updates RFC 5036 to say so and specifies the advertisement mode for all FEC types defined at the time.

plainLanguage.summary: Two routers agree on one way of handing out labels when they start a session. That agreement does not settle everything, because some kinds of traffic always behave in a fixed way. This document says which is which, and lists the rule for every kind of traffic defined so far.

subtitle: Clarifies that the kind of FEC, not only the session's negotiated mode, decides how an LDP speaker advertises labels.

tldr.problem: LDP lets two routers negotiate one label advertisement mode per session, but for some FEC types the advertising behavior is set by the FEC type itself, and the specifications did not say which was which.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7358 updates RFC 5036 to say that the negotiated mode is only indicative, requires every document defining an LDP FEC to state its advertisement discipline, and fills in that discipline for every FEC type defined at the time.
tldr.outcome: Each FEC type now has a stated discipline, one of DU, DoD, as negotiated, upstream, not applicable or unknown, which removes ambiguity when several FEC types share one LDP session.

today: RFC 7358 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the document that updates RFC 3212, RFC 4447, RFC 5036, RFC 5918, RFC 6388 and RFC 7140 on this point.

sections.title: Why the Negotiated Mode Is Only a Hint
sections.content:
The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) (RFC 5036) allows label advertisement mode negotiation at the time of session establishment. The LDP specification also dictates that only a single label advertisement mode be negotiated, agreed upon, and used for a given LDP session between two Label Switching Routers (LSRs).

RFC 7358 explains that the negotiated mode defined in RFC 5036 and carried in the LDP Initialization message is only indicative. It indicates how the LDP speakers on a session will advertise labels for some Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs), but it is not a rule that restricts the speakers to behave in a specific way. For some FEC types, the advertising behavior of the LDP speaker is governed by the FEC type and not by the negotiated behavior.

The document updates RFC 5036 to make that fact clear. It also updates RFC 3212, RFC 4447, RFC 5918, RFC 6388 and RFC 7140 by specifying, for each FEC type that has already been defined, whether the label binding advertisements for that FEC are constrained by the negotiated label advertisement mode or not. It also specifies the label advertisement mode to be used for all currently defined FECs.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers agree on one way of handing out labels when they start a session. That agreement does not settle everything, because some kinds of traffic always behave in a fixed way. This document says which is which.

sections.title: The Six Label Advertisement Disciplines
sections.content:
To remove any ambiguity and conflict regarding a label advertisement discipline among different FEC types sharing a common LDP session, the document introduces a set of types for specifying the label advertisement discipline of a FEC type.

There are six. DU stands for Downstream Unsolicited, DoD for Downstream on Demand, and As negotiated (DU or DoD) for the cases where the mode agreed for the session applies. Upstream refers to upstream label assignment, as defined in RFC 6389. Not applicable covers a FEC type for which the negotiated discipline does not apply, and Unknown covers a FEC type whose discipline has not been stated.

The document defines these six as the vocabulary for stating a discipline. The behavior behind each FEC type itself comes from the RFC that defines that FEC type, which is recorded as the reference for that entry in the registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Every kind of traffic now has to be given one of six labels describing how its labels are offered. Some follow what the two routers agreed. Others have a fixed rule, such as only offering labels when asked, or offering them whether asked or not.

sections.title: The Update to RFC 5036
sections.content:
Section 3.5.3 of RFC 5036 is updated with two added statements under the description of A, Label Advertisement Discipline.

The first says that each document defining an LDP FEC must state the applicability of the negotiated label advertisement discipline for the label binding advertisements for that FEC. If the negotiated label advertisement discipline does not apply to the FEC, the document must also explicitly state the discipline to be used for the FEC. The second statement gives the discipline for two FEC types: the Wildcard FEC, type 0x01, is Not applicable, and the Prefix FEC, type 0x02, is As negotiated, that is DU or DoD.

The rule for future FEC definitions is therefore short: say whether the negotiated discipline applies, and if it does not, say which discipline to use instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The main LDP specification now requires every document that defines a new kind of traffic to state which rule applies to it, and to name a different rule when the session's agreement does not apply.

sections.title: The Discipline for Each FEC Type
sections.content:
The label advertisement discipline for the currently defined LDP FEC types is listed in the registry reproduced in the next section, and the document updates the respective RFCs in which those FECs are introduced and defined.

Reading the list, the Wildcard FEC and the Typed Wildcard FEC Element are Not applicable, since the negotiated discipline does not apply to them. The Prefix FEC follows the negotiated mode. The CR-LSP FEC is Downstream on Demand. The point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-multipoint FECs, the hub-and-spoke FECs, the pseudowire FEC elements and the protection FEC element are Downstream Unsolicited, with the downstream half of the hub-and-spoke FEC also allowing Upstream. The two point-to-multipoint pseudowire FEC elements are Upstream and Downstream Unsolicited respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: The list assigns a rule to each kind of traffic. Prefix traffic follows what the routers agreed. Traffic for a constraint-based path is labelled only when asked. Most multicast traffic is labelled whether asked or not.

sections.title: The Updated IANA Registry
sections.content:
The document mandates the specification of a label advertisement discipline for each defined FEC type, so the IANA Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) Type Name Space registry, under the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) Parameters registry, has been extended. A new column titled Label Advertisement Discipline was added, with the possible values DU, DoD, As negotiated (DU or DoD), Upstream, Not applicable and Unknown. This document was made an additional reference for the registry itself and for all affected registrations, and the other columns were kept in place and populated as they were.

The updated registry lists the FEC types already assigned: 0x01 Wildcard, 0x02 Prefix, 0x04 CR-LSP, 0x05 Typed Wildcard FEC Element, 0x06 P2MP, 0x07 MP2MP-up, 0x08 MP2MP-down, 0x09 HSMP-upstream, 0x0A HSMP-downstream, 0x80 PWid FEC Element, 0x81 Generalized PWid FEC Element, 0x82 P2MP PW Upstream FEC Element, 0x83 Protection FEC Element and 0x84 P2MP PW Downstream FEC Element. Value 0 is reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of traffic kinds gained a column showing the rule for each one, and this document is now cited as the source for that column.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document only clarifies the applicability of an LDP session's label advertisement mode. It therefore adds no LDP security mechanics and no new considerations to those already defined in the LDP specification (RFC 5036).
sections.plainLanguage: The document changes no security behavior. It only says which rule applies, so the security considerations stay exactly as they were in the main LDP specification.

items.title: One mode per session
items.text: RFC 5036 dictates that a single label advertisement mode is negotiated, agreed upon and used for a session.

items.title: The mode is indicative
items.text: The mode in the Initialization message indicates how labels are advertised, but does not restrict the speakers.

items.title: The type can decide
items.text: For some FEC types the advertising behavior is governed by the FEC type, not by the negotiated mode.

items.title: Every FEC document must state it
items.text: Each document defining an LDP FEC must say whether the negotiated discipline applies and, if not, which discipline to use.

items.title: Six possible values
items.text: DU, DoD, As negotiated (DU or DoD), Upstream, Not applicable and Unknown.

items.title: The registry grew a column
items.text: The IANA FEC Type Name Space registry now carries the discipline for each assigned type.
